readerTitle: Guests say the wait is too long. Which wait?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑, 레시피 앱) + 널리 전해지는 일화 (엘리베이터와 거울) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 해결책을 찾기 전에 무엇이, 언제, 얼마나, 목표와 비교해 어떻게 잘못됐는지 적으면 엉뚱한 해결책에 돈을 쓰지 않는다.
misconception: 불만이 들리면 문제는 이미 분명하다. 바로 해결책을 고르면 된다. ("직원이 더 필요하다" 같은 말은 문제가 아니라 해결책이다.)

sources.text: 엘리베이터와 거울 일화: 경영·문제해결 문헌에서 여러 버전으로 전해지는 이야기 (원출처 불분명)
레스토랑과 레시피 앱 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 레스토랑 수치는 가상입니다. 계산 확인: 주문까지 5분 + 음식 14분 + 계산 16분 = 총 35분. 가장 긴 대기는 주방(14분)이 아니라 계산(16분)입니다.
엘리베이터 거울 일화는 출처가 불분명하고 과장되었을 수 있습니다. 카드에 "a story told in many versions", "reportedly", "may be embellished"로 일화임을 표시했습니다. 특정 건물·회사명은 쓰지 않았습니다.
요리사 인건비 월 $3,500은 설명용 가정입니다. 실제 임금 수준을 주장하지 않습니다.

cards.title: Guests say the wait is too long. Which wait?
body: A busy neighborhood restaurant keeps hearing the same complaint on weekend nights: *the wait is too long*.
The owner is ready to hire another cook for $3,500 a month. It feels like the obvious fix. A stopwatch is about to show it would have been money spent on the wrong wait.

image.label: Restaurant table with a stopwatch beside the plates
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 저녁 레스토랑 테이블 위에 접시와 커다란 스톱워치. 손님 두 명이 시계를 보며 지루한 표정. 배경에 바쁜 주방. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you do first?
body: Reviews and comments say guests wait too long on Friday and Saturday nights. Your head chef says the kitchen is stretched. You have budget for one change this month.

options.text: Hire another cook to speed up the kitchen
options.feedback: A cook speeds up the kitchen. If the long wait is somewhere else, you'd pay $3,500 a month and guests would still complain.

options.text: Time each step of a meal for a few busy nights, then pick a fix
options.feedback: It delays the fix by a week but costs almost nothing, and it tells you which wait to fix. Next card shows what it found.

options.text: Serve free bread so the wait feels shorter
options.feedback: Cheap, and it can make the first wait feel shorter. It won't help if guests are annoyed at a different point in the meal.

cards.title: Where the 35 minutes went.
body: The kitchen wasn't the biggest wait. Guests spent **16 minutes** waiting to pay, more than they waited for food. One server was carrying every bill to a single card machine by the bar.

breakdown.label: Order to food
breakdown.detail: The part the cook would fix

breakdown.label: Asking for the bill to paid
breakdown.detail: Waiting for the bill and the card machine

cards.title: Define the problem first
body: **Defining the problem** means writing down exactly what is wrong before you look for fixes: what is happening, when, how much, and compared with what you want.

A useful test: the statement should contain no solution. "We need another cook" is a solution in disguise. "On weekend nights, guests wait about 16 minutes to pay, and we want it under 5" is a problem.
The second version points straight at the bill, not the kitchen.

image.label: A vague complaint turned into a precise problem statement
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 흐릿한 말풍선 "The wait is too long". 오른쪽 선명한 카드에 "What: wait to pay / When: Fri–Sat nights / How much: 16 min / Goal: under 5 min". 가운데 화살표.

cards.title: The way you state a problem picks your solutions.
body: A story told in many versions: tenants of an office building complained the elevators were too slow. Stated as "make the elevators faster," every option was costly.
Someone restated it as "people are bored and impatient while they wait." Mirrors went up beside the elevators, and complaints reportedly dropped. The story may be embellished.
The lesson holds anyway. Each way of stating a problem opens some solutions and quietly hides others.

image.label: People checking themselves in a mirror beside elevator doors
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 엘리베이터 문 옆 큰 거울 앞에서 사람들이 머리를 정리하거나 넥타이를 고치는 장면. 엘리베이터 층수 표시는 그대로. 실제 건물이나 브랜드 표시는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Spot the solution hiding in the sentence.
body: Many "problems" in meetings are really fixes someone already likes. Try rewriting them:
list: "We need more staff" → which tasks are late, by how much, and when?
"We need a new website" → what are visitors failing to do, and how often?
"We need to cut prices" → which deals are we losing, to whom, and at what price gap?
cards.callout: If the sentence names a fix, you haven't defined the problem yet.

cards.title: Define it well enough, then move.
body: Defining a problem should take minutes or days, not weeks. A few nights with a stopwatch was enough here. Some problems only get clear once you try something small, so write your best guess and revise it.
Also, a clear definition tells you *what* hurts, not *why*. Knowing guests wait 16 minutes to pay doesn't yet explain the cause. Finding causes is a separate step.

cards.title: Now it's a recipe app.
body: App store reviews keep saying "the app is slow." Your engineers propose rebuilding the backend, which would take about three months.

options.text: Approve the rebuild. Speed matters to users
options.feedback: You'd bet three months on a guess. If the slowness lives on one screen, most of the rebuild fixes nothing users notice.

options.text: Find which screens are slow, on which devices, by how many seconds, against a target
options.feedback: It costs a few days of data before acting. It may show one search screen taking 8 seconds on older phones, a much smaller fix.

options.text: Add friendly loading animations so waits feel shorter
options.feedback: Like the mirrors, it's cheap and can ease mild waits. But if one screen takes 8 seconds, you've hidden the problem, not fixed it.

cards.title: Write the problem down before you buy the fix.
body: What is happening, when, how much, and compared with what goal. No solution in the sentence.
**Try it today:** take the next "we need…" you hear at work. Rewrite it as a problem with a number and a goal, then see if the original fix still makes sense.
